"async" is also a "
This attribute does not exist: the browser ignores it and loads the image right away.

exercises.explain: A 304 is a response with no body: the browser asked "has this file changed?", the server said no, and the cached copy is reused. A full file comes with a 200.
exercises.prompt: In the DevTools Network tab, a "304 Not Modified" status on "gtm.js" means the server sent the full file again.

exercises.explain: Reading a URL parameter is not dangerous by itself; the danger appears when untrusted data is interpreted as HTML by "innerHTML". With "textContent", the same line would be safe.
exercises.prompt: This results page displays the searched word, taken from the URL. One line makes it vulnerable to code injection (XSS). Which one?

exercises.explain: "dataLayer" is a plain JavaScript array: "push" appends an object to it, and GTM listens to these additions to fire its tags based on the "event" value.
exercises.prompt: Build the line that pushes to the GTM data layer an object whose "event" key is "lead".

exercises.explain: An A record maps a name to an IP address; a CNAME makes a name an alias of another name, here the blog host’s.
exercises.prompt: Here are two DNS records. Where does "blog.example.com" point?
whyWrong: The IP address "203.0.113.10" belongs to the A record of "www", not to the blog.
Nothing links the blog to "www": each line is independent.
The CNAME points exactly to the name written on the right, "sites.headlesscms.io".

exercises.explain: With client-side rendering (CSR), the HTML received is an empty shell that JavaScript fills; whoever does not run JavaScript sees only the shell.
exercises.prompt: What does a bot that reads this HTML without running JavaScript see?
choices: An empty "div", with no heading at all
whyWrong: The heading only exists after the script runs; without JavaScript it is never injected.
The string lives inside the script, not in the page content: a bot does not show it as text.
The server did answer with a valid page; it is just empty of content.

exercises.explain: "X-Cache: HIT" says the copy comes from the CDN and "Age" gives, in seconds, how long it has been there; "max-age" sets its total lifetime.
exercises.prompt: Here are the headers received for the showcase site’s home page. Where does this response come from?
choices: From the CDN cache, where it has been stored for 1 hour
From the origin server, generated just now
From the CDN cache, where it has been stored for 24 hours
From the CDN cache, still valid for 1 hour

code.src:
HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html
cache-control: max-age=86400
x-cache: HIT
age: 3600

whyWrong: "x-cache: HIT" means precisely that the CDN served its copy without asking the origin; a "MISS" would have meant the opposite.
24 hours (86400 s) is the maximum lifetime announced by "cache-control", not the copy’s current age.
"age: 3600" is the time already spent in cache; 86400 minus 3600 seconds remain, that is 23 hours.

exercises.explain: "loading='lazy'" on an image or an iframe postpones its download until it nears the visible area; script-related values do not apply here.
exercises.prompt: This image sits at the very bottom of a long page. What replaces "___" so it is only downloaded when the user scrolls near it?
whyWrong: "eager" is the default behavior: the image is downloaded immediately, wherever it is.
"defer" is an attribute of "<script>", not a value accepted by "loading".
"async" also belongs to scripts; for "loading" it is ignored and the image loads right away.

exercises.explain: A "Disallow" rule forbids any path that starts exactly with the given prefix; everything else is crawled, and "Sitemap" is only a hint.
exercises.prompt: Here is the site’s "robots.txt". Which path must a bot that honors this file NOT crawl?

code.src:
User-agent: *
Disallow: /admin/
Disallow: /preview/
Allow: /

Sitemap: https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml

whyWrong: "/blog/" appears in no "Disallow" rule: the "Allow: /" rule permits it.
"Disallow: /admin/" blocks paths that start with "/admin/" including its slash; "/admin-guide" does not start that way.
The "Sitemap" line tells bots where to find the site map; it does not forbid it, quite the opposite.

exercises.explain: A "fetch" request does not reload the page: the JSON response is converted into an object, then only the targeted element is updated.
exercises.prompt: The server answers with JSON whose count field is 42. What does the "#leads" element contain once the response arrives?
whyWrong: "r.json()" turns the JSON text into an object; the raw text is not inserted, the "count" property is.
"[object Object]" would appear if the whole "data" were inserted; here "data.count" is read, which is 42.
"undefined" would come from a missing property; "count" does exist in the response.

exercises.explain: A headless CMS delivers JSON with no presentation; the front end turns it into HTML, often with "map" then "join('')".
exercises.prompt: These posts come from the headless CMS API. What does this code print?
whyWrong: The comma is the default separator of "join()" with no argument; "join('')" glues the pieces with nothing in between.
"map" applies the template to every post, not just the first one.
"[object Object]" would appear when inserting the whole object; here its "slug" and "title" properties are read.

exercises.explain: With SSR, the server assembles the full page and sends it filled in; with CSR, it sends a shell that JavaScript fills afterwards. That is why SSR is safer for SEO.
exercises.prompt: With server-side rendering (SSR), the HTML received by the browser already contains the posts’ text before any JavaScript runs.

exercises.explain: A CNAME always points to another name, never to an IP address: for an IP you need an A record. TXT records are used for verifications (Search Console, email).
exercises.prompt: One line of this DNS zone is invalid and will be rejected. Which one?

exercises.explain: "fetch" returns a promise of a response; ".then(r => r.json())" reads its body and converts it into an object, whereas "text()" would only give a string.
exercises.prompt: Build a line that requests "/api/posts" then converts the JSON response into a JavaScript object.

exercises.explain: Specificity beats order: one id (1,0,0) outweighs any number of classes, and file order only breaks ties between selectors of equal weight.
exercises.prompt:
HTML: "

49 €

". What color is the price displayed in?
whyWrong: It is the last rule in the file, but order only matters when specificity is equal: a selector with an id weighs more.
It is the first rule: it is overridden by the next two, one more specific, the other written later.
Conflicting rules do not cancel out: the cascade always picks one, here "#hero .price".

exercises.explain: "min-width: X" means "from X px wide upwards": below that threshold only the base rule applies, and "rem" multiplies the root font size.
exercises.prompt: The viewport is 600 px wide. What is the computed font size, in pixels, of the ".cta" button?
whyWrong: 16 px is the root size, not the button’s: "0.875rem" is 0.875 × 16 = 14 px.
"min-width: 768px" only applies from 768 px wide upwards; at 600 px the rule is ignored.
That is the value for screens at least 1024 px wide, far from 600 px.

exercises.explain: A CSS variable is inherited like a color: "var()" reads the value set on the element itself or, failing that, on the closest ancestor, ":root" being only the starting point.
exercises.prompt: HTML: "<section class="hero"><button class="cta">Try it</button></section>". What background color does the button have?
whyWrong: That is the value set on ":root", but ".cta" redefines "--brand" for itself: the closest definition wins.
"--accent" exists but no rule uses it for the background.
A defined variable is never invalid: "var(--brand)" does find a value, the one set on ".cta".

exercises.explain: "1vw" = 1% of the viewport width, "1rem" = the root font size, "%" on "font-size" = the parent’s font size: three relative units, three different references.
exercises.prompt: The viewport is 1000 px wide and no other rule touches the font. What replaces "___" so the heading is exactly 40 px?
whyWrong: "4rem" is 4 × 16 = 64 px: "rem" depends on the root font size, not on the viewport width.
On "font-size", a percentage refers to the parent’s font size: 40% of 16 px is 6.4 px.
"1vw" is 1% of the viewport width, 10 px here: "0.4vw" is only 4 px.

exercises.explain: "repeat(n, 1fr)" creates n columns sharing the space equally; "auto" sizes each column by its content and "3fr" alone makes a single column.
exercises.prompt: ".products" is already "display: grid". Build the declaration that gives it exactly 3 columns of equal width.

exercises.explain: A flex line takes items as long as the sum of their sizes plus the "gap"s between them does not exceed the container; "flex: 0 0 300px" freezes the width, so no shrinking to squeeze in one more card.
exercises.prompt: ".cards" is 960 px wide (no padding) and contains 5 ".card". How many cards fit on the first line?

code.src:
.cards { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 40px; }
.card { flex: 0 0 300px; }

whyWrong: 3 × 300 = 900 px would fit, but the two "gap"s between three cards add 80 px: 980 px exceeds 960 px.
"flex-wrap: wrap" allows wrapping and "flex: 0 0 300px" forbids the cards from shrinking: they cannot all fit.
"gap" is only added between cards, not at the edges: two cards and one gap make 640 px, which fits.

exercises.explain: "fr" units share the leftover space: container width, minus fixed tracks, minus the "gap"s (n − 1 for n columns), the rest divided by the total number of "fr".
exercises.prompt: ".layout" is 800 px wide (no padding) and its cells hold short text. What computed width does each "1fr" column get?
whyWrong: (800 − 240) / 2 forgets the gutters: three columns have two 20 px "gap"s, so 40 px must be removed first.
Only one "gap" was counted; between three columns there are two.
"1fr" does not copy the first column: it is a share of the space left once fixed tracks and "gap"s are removed.

exercises.explain: "repeat()" requires a comma between the repeat count and the track: "repeat(3, 1fr)". A malformed value makes the whole declaration invalid, the browser ignores it and the grid keeps a single implicit column.
exercises.prompt: The product grid shows a single column instead of three. Which line is to blame?

exercises.explain: An "@media" block adds no specificity: when several match, the rule written last wins. So order "max-width" queries from largest to smallest (and "min-width" ones from smallest to largest).
exercises.prompt: The viewport is 500 px wide. How many columns does the ".grid" grid have?
whyWrong: The "max-width: 599px" query does match 500 px, but so does the 1023 px one, and it is written later: with equal specificity, the last one wins.
That is the base rule, overridden by the two media queries which both match 500 px.
No rule defines three columns; CSS does not compromise between two values.

exercises.explain: CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures how much visible content moves; a block whose size is known before it loads already occupies its place, so nothing moves when it appears.
exercises.prompt: Reserving in advance the space of an element that loads later (image, banner, ad) with "height", "min-height" or "aspect-ratio" prevents its appearance from pushing the content below: that is how you reduce CLS.

exercises.explain: "rem" (root em) is always computed from the font size of the "html" element: 2rem with a 16px root gives 32px.
exercises.prompt:
The text sits in "

". What is its computed font size?
whyWrong: "2rem" is not ignored: it is twice the root size, not the root size itself.
"rem" is not a pixel: it is a multiple of the font size of "html".
24px would be "1.5rem" with a 16px root.

exercises.explain: ":hover" applies rules while the pointer is over the element; "transition" on the affected property makes the change gradual, in both directions.
exercises.prompt: What happens when the user hovers over the ".btn" button?
choices: The background fades from #e63946 to #1d3557 over 0.3 s; the text stays white.
The background turns #1d3557 instantly; the transition only plays on the way back.
The text turns #1d3557 over 0.3 s; the background does not change.
Nothing moves for 0.3 s, then the background switches to #1d3557 at once.
whyWrong: The transition applies as soon as the value changes, both in and out.
"background" sets the background, not "color": the text keeps its white color.
0.3s here is the duration of the change, not a delay before it starts.

exercises.explain: "font-family" is a fallback list: the browser takes the first available font, left to right, and the final generic keyword guarantees a consistent look.
exercises.prompt: "Promo Display" is neither installed on the user's device nor loaded with "@font-face"; Georgia is installed. Which font is used for the banner text?
choices: The browser's default font, the rule being ignored
whyWrong: The "serif" keyword is only used as a last resort, when none of the fonts named before it is available.
The browser never downloads a font on its own: without "@font-face", an unknown name is simply skipped.
A missing font does not invalidate the rule: the browser moves on to the next one in the list.

exercises.explain: "em" is computed from the parent's font size and compounds through nesting; "rem" always goes back to "html", whatever the parent.
exercises.prompt:
HTML: "
Deal: 29 €
". What is the computed font size of the price?
whyWrong: 30px would be "1.5em": "em" is based on the parent (20px), but "rem" is based on the root (10px).
20px is the banner's size; the price has its own rule, it does not simply inherit.
24px assumes a 16px root, but "html" is set to 10px here.

exercises.explain: "prefers-color-scheme: dark" only changes what you redefine inside it: remember to adjust every color variable, background and text, or the contrast disappears.
exercises.prompt: The user has enabled dark mode on their system. What colors does the banner get?
choices: Background #111111, text #111111: the text becomes invisible
Background #111111, text in the browser's default color
whyWrong: Nothing inverts colors automatically: only "--bg" is redefined in the media query, "--ink" keeps #111111.
The media query does match the user's setting: its redefinition of "--bg" wins, as it comes later with the same specificity.
"--ink" is still defined (#111111): "var(--ink)" therefore has a value and the browser has nothing to replace.

exercises.explain: In the "animation" shorthand, the duration carries a time unit and the iteration count has none; the total time is duration × iterations, and without "fill-mode" the element goes back to its original style at the end.
exercises.prompt: What does the user see on the ".cta" button when the page loads?
choices: It grows by 10% and back, 3 times (6 s in total), then keeps its normal size.
It grows and shrinks back in a loop, indefinitely, every 2 s.
It grows once over 2 s and stays enlarged at 110%.
It grows and shrinks back 3 times, 3 s in total, at 1 s per cycle.
whyWrong: The number "3" in the shorthand is the iteration count; an endless loop would need "infinite".
The animation plays 3 times, and "to" goes back to "scale(1)": without "animation-fill-mode", the button returns to its normal size.
"2s" is the duration of each cycle and "3" the number of cycles: 3 × 2 s = 6 s.

exercises.explain: In the "transition" shorthand, the first time value is always the duration and the second the delay ("transition-delay").
exercises.prompt: On hover, the background must wait 300 ms, then change gradually over 1 s. What goes in place of "___"?
whyWrong: Order matters: the first time is the transition duration, the second the delay; here the background would wait 1 s then change over 300 ms.
The comma separates two distinct transitions; it is not how you specify a delay.
A single time gives a 1.3 s transition that starts right away, with no waiting time.

exercises.explain: "opacity" applies to the whole element, content included, and no child can become opaque again; to fade only the background, use a color with an alpha channel, such as "rgb(0 0 0 / 0.5)".
exercises.prompt: With ".banner { opacity: 0.5; color: #ffffff; }", the white text inside the banner is also rendered half transparent, not just the background.

exercises.explain: A hex color has 3, 4, 6 or 8 digits after "#"; with 5 digits the declaration is invalid and the text keeps its inherited color. "hsl(210 80% 50%)" and "font-weight: 700" are perfectly valid.
exercises.prompt: One declaration is invalid and will be ignored by the browser. Which one?

exercises.explain: In "hsl()" the order is fixed: hue, saturation, lightness, then "/" and the alpha (0 to 1); the alpha fades only that color, unlike "opacity", which fades the whole element.
exercises.prompt: Build a declaration that gives a pure red background (hue 0, saturation 100%, lightness 50%) at 50% opacity, using "hsl" notation.

exercises.explain: "clamp(min, value, max)" keeps the middle value as long as it stays between the two bounds: 1vw is 1% of the viewport width, so 5vw is 60px at 1200px and only 20px at 400px, where the 32px floor takes over.
exercises.prompt: The root font size is 16px. What is the computed size of this landing page title on a 1200px wide viewport?
whyWrong: 64px is the ceiling (4rem): it only applies when 5vw exceeds it, and 5% of 1200px is 60px.
32px is the floor (2rem): it only applies on a small screen, when 5vw drops below 32px (viewport of 640px or less).
5vw is not 5 × 16px: "vw" is relative to the viewport width, not to the root font size.

exercises.explain: A unitless "line-height" is a factor multiplied by each element’s font size; that is why it is preferred over px or %: children with a different font size recompute their own line height.
exercises.prompt: The root font size is 16px. What line height, in px, does this intro paragraph get?
whyWrong: 24px would be 1.5 × 16px: the factor applies to the element’s own font size (20px), not to the root font size.
A unitless value is perfectly valid for "line-height": the declaration is not ignored.
Without a unit, 1.5 is a multiplier of the font size, not a length of 1.5px.

exercises.explain: "text-transform" changes the displayed case without touching the HTML; it is often paired with a "letter-spacing" in em, which adds a space proportional to the font size between the letters of an all-caps eyebrow.
exercises.prompt:
The HTML contains "

black friday

". The user must read "BLACK FRIDAY" with spaced-out letters. What goes in place of "___"?
whyWrong: "capitalize" only uppercases the first letter of each word: you would read "Black Friday".
"small-caps" is a value of "font-variant", not of "text-transform": the declaration would be invalid and ignored.
"lowercase" forces everything to lowercase: the text would stay "black friday".

exercises.explain: "rem" is always relative to the root element’s ("html") font size, whatever the parents: that is what makes a type scale in rem predictable and resizable in one place.
exercises.prompt: The browser default font size is 16px. What is the computed size of the "h2"?
whyWrong: 24px would be 1.5 × 16px: the rule on "html" changed the root font size, which is 125% of 16px, that is 20px.
22.5px would be 1.5 × 15px, the "body" size: that is how "em" works, not "rem", which ignores intermediate parents.
20px is the root font size itself; the "h2" takes 1.5 times that.

exercises.explain: In normal flow, a block’s bottom margin and the next block’s top margin collapse: the space equals the larger of the two. In a flex or grid container they do not collapse, and "gap" adds to the margins.
exercises.prompt:
The HTML contains, in normal flow, "

Launch offer

" followed by "

Save 20% this week.

". What distance separates the bottom of the "h1" from the top of the "p"?
whyWrong: The vertical margins of two consecutive blocks do not add up: they collapse and only the larger one counts.
The "p" rule does not override the "h1" rule: both margins exist and the larger one, 32px, wins.
Margins are not subtracted: collapsing keeps the maximum value, not the difference.

exercises.explain: "aspect-ratio" sets the box (here 200 × 200px from the width) and "object-fit" decides how the image sits inside it: "contain" shrinks it without distortion until it fully fits, "cover" crops it to fill everything.
exercises.prompt: The product visual "" is 400 × 200px originally. How does the image appear inside its box?
choices: Shrunk to 200 × 100px, centered, with 50px empty at the top and bottom
Kept at 400 × 200px, cropped by 100px on the left and right
whyWrong: That is the rendering of "object-fit: fill" (the default value); "contain" preserves the image proportions.
That is the rendering of "object-fit: cover", which fills the box and crops the excess; "contain" fits the whole image inside.
With "object-fit", the image is always clipped to its box; only "none" keeps the original size, and even then it does not overflow.

exercises.explain: "scale" enlarges around "transform-origin" (the center by default), so a 200px box grown to 300px spills 50px on each side; "translateX(100px)" then shifts everything 100px to the right, without being scaled itself.
exercises.prompt: Without any transform, this visual spans horizontally from 0 to 200px. "transform-origin" keeps its default value. Between which x positions does the visual appear once transformed?
whyWrong: That would be the result if the scaling started from the left edge; by default the origin is the center, so the box gains 50px on each side.
That is the translation alone: "scale(1.5)" also widens the box from 200 to 300px.
Here the translation is not multiplied by 1.5: the shift stays 100px and the scaling happens around the center, not the left edge.

exercises.explain: "ch" is a font-relative unit, like "em": that is what lets you cap a line length in an approximate number of characters (45 to 75 for comfortable reading), whatever the text size.
exercises.prompt: With "max-width: 65ch" on a paragraph, the maximum width in pixels depends on the paragraph’s font and text size, because "ch" is the width of the digit "0" in that font.

exercises.explain: "rotate()" requires an angle with its unit ("45deg", "0.125turn"); only zero may be written without a unit. Conversely, a unitless "line-height: 1.4" is valid, and "aspect-ratio" is indeed written with a slash.
exercises.prompt: In this rule for a tilted product visual, one declaration is invalid and will be ignored by the browser. Which one?

exercises.explain: "left: 50%" puts the top-left corner at the parent’s center; the percentages of "translate" are relative to the box itself, so "translate(-50%, -50%)" pulls it back by half its width and height, whatever its size.
exercises.prompt: A box is positioned with "position: absolute; left: 50%; top: 50%". Build the declaration that recenters it exactly on its own center.

exercises.explain: In BEM, "block__element" ties an element to its block and "--modifier" describes a variant: the component's structure can be read in the class name.
exercises.prompt: The "hero" component follows the BEM convention. Which class names its button (element "cta") in its "primary" variant?
whyWrong: Two underscores introduce an element, not a modifier: BEM never nests two elements in one name.
The order is reversed: "--" marks a modifier and "__" an element, so "hero--cta" would be a variant of the whole block.
Single hyphens separate the words of one name ("call-to-action"); they do not distinguish block, element and modifier.

exercises.explain: In native nesting, "&" stands for the parent selector: joined to a class it stacks conditions on the same element; separated by a space it targets a descendant.
exercises.prompt: Which classic selector is the nested rule "&.nav--dark" equivalent to?
whyWrong: A space between "&" and the class would give a descendant; here the two classes are joined, so they sit on the same element.
The "&" is not decorative: it inserts the parent selector ".nav", so the element must carry both classes.
The ">" combinator appears nowhere; "&" joined to a class creates no parent-child relationship.

exercises.explain: "A:has(B)" selects A when a matching B exists inside it: it is a parent selector, the condition concerns descendants but the style applies to A.
exercises.prompt:
HTML: "
Starter
Pro
Team
". Which element gets the gold border?
whyWrong: ":has()" qualifies the element before the parenthesis, not the one inside it: the badge is the condition, not the target.
Only the plan that actually contains a ".badge" meets the condition; Starter and Team keep the gray border.
The section does contain a badge, but it lacks the "plan" class: the selector does not apply to it.

exercises.explain: Between two layers, the layer declared last wins whatever the specificity; that is what lets very simple utilities override components.
exercises.prompt:
HTML: "
". What padding does the link have?
choices: It depends on the order of the two "@layer" blocks in the file
The browser's default padding: the two rules cancel out
whyWrong: ".hero .cta" is more specific, but layers are compared before specificity: "utilities", declared last, wins.
The layer order is fixed by the first line "@layer components, utilities;"; moving the blocks would change nothing.
Two conflicting declarations never cancel out: the cascade always picks one.

exercises.explain: An unnamed "@container" is evaluated against the nearest ancestor that has a "container-type"; the window and farther containers play no part.
exercises.prompt: "main" is 1200px wide and contains a 300px wide ".sidebar"; a ".card" sits inside the ".sidebar" and the window is 1400px wide. What "display" does the ".card" have?
choices: flex, only because the window is wider than 400px
Undefined: two containers contradict each other
whyWrong: "main" is indeed 1200px wide, but "@container" queries the element's nearest container: here the 300px ".sidebar".
The window width only matters for "@media"; "@container" ignores the viewport.
There is no conflict: each element is evaluated only against its nearest ancestor container.

exercises.explain: A "var()" is resolved on the element where the property is declared, and that computed value is what gets inherited: redefining "--brand" lower down does not recompute "--cta-bg".
exercises.prompt:
HTML: "
". What background color does the button have?
whyWrong: "--cta-bg" was resolved on ":root", where "--brand" is "#0a5"; the button inherits that already computed value, not the formula "var(--brand)".
That would be the value if "--cta-bg" were defined nowhere; but ".cta" inherits it from ":root".
An inherited custom property is perfectly valid; "var(--cta-bg)" is substituted without error.

exercises.explain: Layers are ordered by first appearance, often fixed by an "@layer a, b;" statement at the top of the file: the last declared layer wins, whatever the order of the blocks that follow.
exercises.prompt: You want the text of ".btn" to be "blue". What goes in place of "___"?
whyWrong: With "base, theme", the "theme" layer is declared last: it wins and the button is red.
Declaring only "base" puts it first; "theme" is created afterwards, in last position, and wins: red.
Adding "reset" changes nothing in the duel: "theme" is still declared after "base" and wins: red.

exercises.explain: It is the other way round: unlayered styles form an implicit layer placed last and beat every declared layer for normal declarations; the order only flips with "!important".
exercises.prompt: Without "!important", a declaration written outside any "@layer" is beaten by any competing declaration placed in a layer, even a less specific one.

exercises.explain: "container-name" only names; without "container-type: inline-size" (or "size"), the element is not a queryable container and the "@container" never applies.
exercises.prompt: The ".card" elements inside ".grid" always stay at "display: block", even when ".grid" is 900px wide. Which line is to blame?

exercises.explain: ":has()" takes a relative selector: "> .badge" requires a direct child, whereas ".badge" alone would accept any descendant.
exercises.prompt: Build the selector that targets every ".plan" that has a ".badge" as a direct child.

exercises.explain: "<title>" gives the title of the tab and bookmarks, and is the basis for the Google result title; the "<h1>" is the heading visible in the page, and the meta description a summary meant for search engines.
exercises.prompt: What text appears in the browser tab?

code.src: Trail Runner X

whyWrong: The "<h1>" is the heading visible in the page; the tab shows the content of "<title>".
The meta description is not displayed by the browser; it serves as a summary for search engines.
The brand name is only part of the "<title>": the tab shows the full text.

exercises.explain: "<nav>" marks a block of major navigation links; screen readers and search engines recognize the menu there, which a "<div>" does not convey.
exercises.prompt: Which semantic tag should replace this "<div>"?
whyWrong: "<header>" groups the introduction of a page or section (logo, heading); it may contain the menu, but it is not the tag for the menu itself.
"<aside>" is for tangential content (side box, related links), not the site's main navigation.
"<section>" is a generic thematic grouping; a block of navigation links has its own dedicated tag.

exercises.explain: "<meta name="robots">" is read directive by directive: "noindex" removes the page from results, "follow" or "nofollow" decides whether its links are followed. For Google to see the tag, the page must not be blocked by robots.txt.
exercises.prompt: Will Google index this campaign page?
choices: No: it stays out of results, but its links are followed
No, and Google does not follow its links either
Yes, but only for the duration of the campaign

code.src:
<head>
  <meta name="robots" content="noindex, follow">
  <title>Black Friday: -30% on all shoes</title>
</head>

whyWrong: The two directives are independent: "follow" allows following the links, "noindex" forbids indexing; one does not cancel the other.
That would be the case with "noindex, nofollow"; here "follow" explicitly asks to follow the links.
No robots directive has a duration: "noindex" applies as long as the tag is in place.

exercises.explain: "lang" on "<html>" sets the language of the whole page; you only override it on elements written in another language, and those exceptions do not extend to their siblings.
exercises.prompt: Which language do screen readers and translation tools assign to the text "Bonjour"?
choices: English, like the paragraph before it
The language of the user's browser
whyWrong:
"lang" applies only to the element carrying it and its descendants; the "
" is not inside the "

".
An element without "lang" inherits the language of its nearest ancestor that has one, here "<html>".
The content language is declared by the page, not deduced from the browser settings.

exercises.explain: A page reachable through several URLs (UTM parameters, sorting, http/https) declares its reference URL with "<link rel="canonical">"; Google consolidates the signals there instead of spreading ranking across duplicates.
exercises.prompt: This product page is served at "https://shop.example/shoes?utm_source=newsletter". Which URL does it ask Google to treat as canonical?

code.src:
<head>
  <title>Trail Runner X</title>
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://shop.example/shoes">
  <meta name="description" content="Lightweight trail shoe, 89 €">
</head>

whyWrong: That is the address actually visited; the canonical tag exists precisely to say this UTM variant is just a copy of the clean URL.
The canonical is the exact URL written in "href", not the site root.
The purpose of "rel="canonical"" is the opposite: to group duplicates under one URL instead of indexing them twice.

exercises.explain: Open Graph tags ("og:title", "og:description", "og:image", "og:url") drive the share preview on social networks; "<title>" and the meta description remain for the tab and search engines.
exercises.prompt: Which title appears in the preview when this post is shared on a social network that reads Open Graph (Facebook, LinkedIn)?
choices: 5 tips to run your first trail

code.src:
<head>
  <title>Blog | Acme Shoes</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Tips for runners">
  <meta property="og:title" content="5 tips to run your first trail">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://acme.example/trail.jpg">
</head>

whyWrong: That is the tab title; social networks read "og:title" first and fall back to "<title>" only when it is missing.
The meta description feeds search engines; the preview description would come from "og:description", absent here.
"og:image" provides the preview image, not its title.
exercises.output: 5 tips to run your first trail

exercises.explain: Without a proper viewport, a phone renders the page like a desktop screen and then shrinks it; "width=device-width, initial-scale=1" matches the layout width to the screen, without zoom: it is the prerequisite for responsive design and Google's mobile-friendliness.
exercises.prompt: This blog post must display at the phone's screen width, without zooming out. What goes in place of ___?
whyWrong: "initial-scale=0.5" opens the page zoomed out by half: the content appears at half size.
A fixed width of 980 px is wider than a phone screen: the browser zooms out to fit everything, as if there were no viewport tag.
"responsive" is not a viewport property; the tag is ignored and the page is rendered at a desktop width then shrunk.

exercises.explain: "rel="nofollow"" is a signal for crawlers: it tells them you do not vouch for the linked page (unverified link, comments) and that no credit should be passed to it; it changes nothing for display or clicking.
exercises.prompt: A link "<a href="https://partner.example" rel="nofollow">" stays clickable and takes the visitor to the target page; the attribute is only aimed at search engines.

exercises.explain: The "<h1>" states the single topic of the page; each sub-part goes down one level ("<h2>", then "<h3>") without skipping any. HTML and Google tolerate several "<h1>", but a single main heading makes the page easier to read for screen readers and clearer for SEO.
exercises.prompt: Best practice: a product page has a single main "<h1>" heading, with its sub-parts going down to "<h2>". Which line breaks this rule?

exercises.explain: The canonical is declared with "<link rel="canonical" href="…">" in the "<head>": a void "<link>" tag with no closing tag, not a "<meta>", and with an absolute URL.
exercises.prompt: Build the tag that declares "https://shop.example/shoes" as the page's canonical URL.

exercises.explain: In a table, each "<tr>" is a row and each cell it holds ("<th>" or "<td>") takes one column; the header row counts as a row.
exercises.prompt: How many rows and columns does this pricing table display?
whyWrong: The header row is also a "<tr>": it counts as a row, even though its cells are "<th>".
Each "<tr>" holds two cells, so two columns; the number of rows does not change the number of columns.
Each "<th>" or "<td>" is a cell, not a row: the rows are the "<tr>" elements.

exercises.explain: Each named field is sent as "name=value"; with "get", those pairs follow the "?" in the URL given by "action".
exercises.prompt: Which URL does the browser request when you click OK?

code.src:
<form action="/subscribe" method="get">
  <input type="text" name="city" value="Lyon">
  <button type="submit">OK</button>
</form>

whyWrong: With "method="get"", the form data is appended to the URL after a "?".
It is the "name" attribute, not "type", that names the field in the URL.
The button has no "name" attribute, so it sends nothing.

exercises.explain: A relative link without a leading "/" resolves from the current page's folder; a link starting with "/" starts from the site root.
exercises.prompt: This link is on the page "/blog/article.html". Where does it lead?
whyWrong: Without a leading "/", the path is relative to the page's folder, here "/blog/", not to the site root.
A relative path replaces the current file name; it is not appended after it.
"article.html" is a file, not a folder: the current folder is "/blog/".

exercises.explain: "for" takes the field's "id", not its "name": "id" identifies the element in the page, "name" is used when sending to the server.
exercises.prompt: In "<label for="email">", the value of "for" must match the "name" attribute of the field to associate.

exercises.explain: A checkbox is only sent when it is checked, and without a "value" attribute its value is "on"; give it a "value" to send something else.
exercises.prompt: You submit this form without touching anything. What data does the server receive?

code.src:
<form action="/lead" method="post">
  <input type="checkbox" name="newsletter" checked>
  <input type="checkbox" name="offers">
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>

whyWrong: An unchecked box is not sent at all, and a checked box without "value" is worth "on", not "true".
An unchecked box is absent from the data: it is not sent with an empty value.
"checked" sets the box's initial state; the default value sent is "on".

exercises.explain: "pattern" requires the whole value to match the regular expression; "AB1" has neither four characters nor only capitals, so the browser refuses to submit and shows a message.
exercises.prompt: You click Send without changing the values. Which field blocks submission?

code.src:
<form action="/contact" method="post">
  <input type="text" name="name" value="Lea" required>
  <input type="email" name="email" value="lea@agency.io" required>
  <input type="text" name="promo" value="AB1" pattern="[A-Z]{4}">
  <input type="text" name="city" value="Lyon" minlength="3">
  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>

whyWrong: "required" only demands a non-empty value, and "Lea" is one.
"lea@agency.io" is a valid address for "type="email"", and the field is not empty.
"Lyon" is 4 characters long, which satisfies "minlength="3"".

exercises.explain: For radio buttons and "<option>" elements, the "value" attribute of the checked or selected element is what goes to the server, in the order of the form's fields.
exercises.prompt: You click Go without changing anything. Which URL is requested?

code.src:
<form action="/quote" method="get">
  <input type="radio" name="plan" value="starter"> Starter
  <input type="radio" name="plan" value="pro" checked> Pro
  <select name="seats">
    <option value="5">1-5</option>
    <option value="20" selected>6-20</option>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Go</button>
</form>

whyWrong: The server receives the "value" attributes, not the text shown next to the button or inside the option.
Two radio buttons sharing the same "name" form a group: only one is checked, so only one is sent.
The option marked "selected" is the one sent, not the first in the list.

exercises.explain: "../" goes up one folder from the current page; from "/blog/", you are back at the root. An absolute path like "/pricing.html" works from any page.
exercises.prompt: This link is on the page "/blog/article.html" and must lead to "/pricing.html". What goes in place of ___?
whyWrong: Without a prefix, the path stays in the "/blog/" folder: you would land on "/blog/pricing.html".
"./" means the current folder, so again "/blog/pricing.html".
This path is appended to the current folder and would give "/blog/blog/pricing.html".

exercises.explain: Only fields with a "name" attribute are sent to the server; "id" is for the "<label>" and CSS, not for submission.
exercises.prompt: The form submits, but the server never receives the typed address. Which line is to blame?

exercises.explain: An "<input>" is a void element with no closing tag: "type" picks the keyboard and validation, "name" is used for submission, and "required" blocks submission while the field is empty.
exercises.prompt: Build a required email field named "email", with the attributes in the order type, name, required.

exercises.explain: "lang" is inherited by descendants, and a "lang" set on an element overrides the inherited one. The screen reader picks its voice from that attribute.
exercises.prompt: In which language does a screen reader pronounce the second paragraph?

code.src:
Bienvenue sur notre boutique.

Free shipping this week!

whyWrong: The "lang="fr"" on "html" applies to the whole document, except for elements that declare their own "lang".
The system language is only used when the page declares none; here two "lang" attributes are declared.
A paragraph is still read whatever its language; "lang" hides nothing, it changes the voice.

exercises.explain: Heading levels form an outline: go down one level at a time (h1, h2, h3…) without skipping, and go back up freely.
exercises.prompt: A screen reader lets you jump from heading to heading with their level. Which heading breaks the hierarchy?
choices: "Leather bags": jumps from h2 to h4, no h3
"Sneakers": an h3 cannot follow an h2
"Shoes": there can be only one h2
whyWrong: An h3 under an h2 is exactly a subsection: that is the expected order.
Several h2 are normal: they are the same-level sections under the h1.
Going from h2 to h4 leaves an empty level: the user looks for an h3 that does not exist.

exercises.explain: Only natively interactive elements ("a href", "button", form fields) and those with "tabindex="0"" enter the tab order; a click handler changes nothing.
exercises.prompt: Which elements can be reached with the Tab key?
whyWrong: "role="button"" and "onclick" do not make a "div" focusable: it would need "tabindex="0"".
"tabindex="0"" puts the "span" into the tab order, just like a link.
A "div" without "tabindex" and a "p" never receive keyboard focus.

exercises.explain: The browser evaluates "sizes" (first true condition, else the last value) to get the displayed width, multiplies it by the DPR, then takes the smallest "w" candidate that reaches that width.
exercises.prompt: Viewport 800 px wide, screen with a DPR of 1. Which image does the browser load?
choices: All three, to pick the sharpest
whyWrong: 800 px is the viewport width, not the image width: at 800 px the "max-width: 600px" condition is false, so the image is 50vw, i.e. 400 px.
1600 px would only be useful with a DPR of 4 for a 400 px slot.
The browser downloads only one candidate, the one that is enough for the slot.

exercises.explain: In "picture", the browser takes the first "source" whose "media" is true, in source order; "img" is the fallback and carries the "alt".
exercises.prompt: Viewport 800 px wide. Which image is displayed?
whyWrong: "min-width: 1000px" is false at 800 px: that source is ignored.
The "img" "src" is only used when no "source" matches.
The browser picks a single source before downloading; it does not chain two.

exercises.explain: "aria-label" gives an element its accessible name and takes precedence over its content; "aria-hidden="true"" hides an element from assistive technology without changing the display.
exercises.prompt: What does a screen reader read for this banner close button?
whyWrong: "aria-hidden="true"" removes the "×" from the accessibility tree: it is never read.
"aria-label" replaces the content as the accessible name; it is not added to it.
Only the "span" is hidden; the button itself keeps the name given by "aria-label".

exercises.explain: "kind="subtitles"" translates or transcribes the dialogue for those who hear the sound; "captions" replaces the sound for those who do not. In both cases the file is in WebVTT format.
exercises.prompt: The product video is in English. This track must display the French translation of the dialogue for viewers who can hear the sound. Which value replaces "___"?

code.src:
<video controls src="product-demo.mp4">
  <track kind="___" src="demo-fr.vtt" srclang="fr" label="Français">
</video>

whyWrong: "captions" targets viewers without sound: the track also transcribes noises and music.
"descriptions" is a text description of the picture, read by speech synthesis for blind people.
"chapters" is for navigating the video, not for showing text on screen.

exercises.explain: Only "alt=""" marks the image as decorative and removes it from the accessibility tree. Without "alt", the image stays exposed and the reader typically announces the file name or "image".
exercises.prompt: True or false: "alt=""" and having no "alt" attribute at all have the same effect; in both cases the screen reader ignores the image.

exercises.explain: Every "iframe" must carry a descriptive "title" ("Product demo video"): it is its accessible name, announced before the user enters the frame.
exercises.prompt: A screen reader announces an unnamed frame in this section. Which line is missing an accessibility attribute?

exercises.explain: The "alt" of an informative image says what it conveys (the promo message), never its file name; "alt=""" or "aria-hidden" would make it ignored.
exercises.prompt: Build the tag of a promo banner that a screen reader announces as "Summer sale: 30% off".

exercises.explain: "map" applies a function to each item and returns a new array without touching the original; "join(sep)" glues the items together with the chosen separator.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: Those are the original prices: "map" returns a new array with the transformed values, and it is "sale" that gets printed.
That is what "join()" gives without an argument; here the separator is " | ".
That would be the array itself being printed; "join" returns a string, with no brackets.

exercises.explain: "JSON.stringify" turns an object into compact JSON text: double-quoted keys, no spaces, types preserved ("true" and "42" stay unquoted).
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?

code.src:
const lead = { email: "ana@shop.com", optin: true, score: 42 };
console.log(JSON.stringify(lead));

whyWrong: That is JavaScript object syntax; in JSON, keys are always wrapped in double quotes.
JSON keeps types: a boolean and a number are not quoted, only strings are.
That is what you get by concatenating an object to a string; "JSON.stringify" produces a readable representation instead.

exercises.explain: "querySelectorAll" returns every element matching the selector at the time of the call; "classList.add" and "contains" change and test classes without overwriting the others.
exercises.prompt: The page has a "#products" list with three "li.product" items: Tee, Cap and Mug; only Cap also has the "sold-out" class. What does this code print?
whyWrong: That is the number of ".product" items; the "hidden" class is only added to items that already have "sold-out".
That would be the number of available items; the "if" targets the sold-out item, not the others.
"classList.add" really adds the class to the DOM: the second "querySelectorAll" sees it because it runs after the loop.

exercises.explain: "filter" keeps the items for which the function returns true and gives back a new, often shorter, array; "map" transforms, "find" looks up a single item, "forEach" returns nothing.
exercises.prompt: Which method replaces "___" so that this code prints 2?
whyWrong: "map" returns an array of the same size (three booleans here), so "length" is 3.
"find" returns the first matching object, not an array: "cheap.length" is "undefined".
"forEach" returns nothing ("undefined"): reading ".length" on it throws an error.

exercises.explain: A click on a child bubbles up to the listening parents; "event.target" is always the element where the click started, "event.currentTarget" the one holding the listener.
exercises.prompt: The newsletter form "#signup" contains an "#email" field and a "#send" button. The user clicks the button. What does the console show?
whyWrong: "signup" is the element that listens ("event.currentTarget"); "event.target" is the element that was actually clicked.
The field was not clicked; "event.target" points to the button, not another child of the form.
The button does have an "id"; the event bubbles up to the form but "target" remains the button.

exercises.explain: "forEach" runs the function for each item and returns "undefined"; it is "map" that builds a new array from the returned values.
exercises.prompt: In JavaScript, "forEach" returns a new array containing the values returned by the function passed to it.

exercises.explain: "JSON.parse" gives values back their real type: "optin" becomes the boolean "true", which has no "toUpperCase" method (TypeError). On the string "email", the call works.
exercises.prompt: One line throws an error. Which one?

exercises.explain: "fetch" returns a promise of a response and "response.json()" a promise of data: two "await" are needed to get the JavaScript object and work on it with array methods.
exercises.prompt: The "/api/leads" API responds with the JSON {"leads": [{"email": "a@shop.com", "optin": true}, {"email": "b@shop.com", "optin": false}]}. What does this code print?
whyWrong: That is the total number of leads; "filter" only keeps those whose "optin" is "true".
"response.json()" does return a promise, but "await" waits for it to resolve and gives the parsed object.
"data.leads" exists in the response and "filter" always returns an array, which has a "length".

exercises.explain: "await" does not block the page: it only pauses the "async" function, the code after the call runs right away, and the function resumes once the promise resolves.
exercises.prompt: In what order do the messages appear?
choices:
track start
page ready
track done

track start
track done
page ready

page ready
track start
track done
whyWrong: That would be the order if "await" blocked the whole script; in fact it yields and the rest of the code keeps running during the 100 ms.
An "async" function runs immediately up to its first "await": "track start" is printed before "track()" yields.
The promise resolves when the "setTimeout" fires, after 100 ms; the function then resumes and prints "track done".
exercises.output:
track start
page ready
track done

exercises.explain: A JSON string received from an API must first go through "JSON.parse" to become an object whose properties you can read; "JSON.stringify" goes the other way.
exercises.prompt: "raw" holds the string '{"count": 3}'. Build a line that prints 3.

exercises.explain: "obj.prop" and "obj["prop"]" read the same property; in a template literal, every "${…}" is replaced by its value.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: Inside backticks, "${…}" is evaluated and replaced by the value; you would get the raw text only with single quotes.
"customer["plan"]" reads the property named plan, whose value is "pro", not the key name.
Bracket notation with a string is the same as dot notation; the property does exist.

exercises.explain: Object destructuring copies properties into same-named variables; "= value" supplies a default used only when the property is missing or undefined.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: Without "= "email"", channel would be undefined; the default value kicks in precisely when the property is missing.
Destructuring creates variables that receive the values, not the key names.
"console.log" prints all three arguments; channel is not skipped, it gets its default value.

exercises.explain: "{ ...a, key: v }" builds a new object with the properties of "a", then "key" overrides the copied value when it comes after; the source object is unchanged.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: In an object literal the last write to a key wins: "budget: 250" comes after the spread and overrides it.
Spread copies the properties into a new object; "base" is left untouched.
It is the other way round: promo gets 250 and base keeps 100.

exercises.explain: Inside a method, "this" is the instance the method was called on; returning "this" lets you chain calls on the same object.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: The second "add" does not replace the first: it pushes into the same "this.items" array, which holds 20 and 15.
"total()" returns the sum computed by "reduce", not the array.
"add" returns "this", so ".add(15)" and ".total()" are called on the cart; nothing returns undefined.

exercises.explain: "?." returns undefined instead of throwing when the left side is null or undefined; "??" only replaces null and undefined, whereas "||" also replaces 0, "" and false.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?

code.src:
const lead = { name: "Max", score: 0 };
console.log(lead.company?.name ?? "unknown", lead.score ?? 10, lead.score || 10);

whyWrong: "??" only replaces null or undefined; 0 is a real value, so it is kept.
"||" replaces any falsy value, and 0 is falsy, so it yields 10.
"lead.company?.name" is indeed undefined, but "?? "unknown"" replaces it right away.

exercises.explain: "{ ...obj }" is a shallow copy: primitives are duplicated, but nested objects and arrays stay shared between the original and the copy.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: Spread only copies the first level: "copy.tags" and "customer.tags" are the same array, so the push affects both.
"name" is a string copied by value; changing "copy.name" does not affect "customer.name".
That would be true if "copy" were the very same object as "customer", but spread does create a new top-level object.

exercises.explain: Only a deep copy ("structuredClone", or JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(…)) for simple data) also duplicates nested objects; spread and "Object.assign" copy the first level only.
exercises.prompt: What should replace "___" so that this code prints 10?
whyWrong: "Object.assign(campaign)" with a single argument returns "campaign" itself, and even with an empty target the copy would be shallow: "stats" would stay shared and print 99.
"Object.freeze" returns the same object, frozen only at the top level: "stats" stays writable and the code prints 99.
"Object.create(campaign)" makes an empty object that inherits from "campaign"; "copy.stats" is then the original object and the output is 99.

exercises.explain: The default export is imported without braces under any name ("import utils from "./utils.js""), hence only one is allowed; named exports are imported in braces with their exact name ("import { total } from …").
exercises.prompt: In an ES module, a file can have only one "export default" but as many named exports ("export const …") as it wants.

exercises.explain: "let" and "const" are block-scoped: "bonus" only exists between the braces of the "if", hence the ReferenceError on the last line. Only "var" would ignore the block.
exercises.prompt: One line raises an error. Which one?

exercises.explain: For a score that can legitimately be 0, use "??": it only replaces null and undefined, whereas "||" would also swap 0 for the fallback.
exercises.prompt: Given "const lead = { score: 0 };", build a line that prints 0 (not 10).

exercises.explain: "map()" always returns a new array of the same length and never mutates the original.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: That would be the case if "map()" changed the original array; it returns a new array and leaves "prices" untouched.
"map()" transforms each element but never changes the count: 3 inputs give 3 outputs.
"prices" is neither emptied nor moved by "map()"; its first element is still 10.

exercises.explain: "reduce()" folds the elements into an accumulator that starts at the initial value; with 0, it is a plain sum.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: JavaScript has a single number type: a whole result prints without ".0".
That gluing would only happen if the initial value were a string; here it is the number 0, so "+" adds.
All values are valid numbers, nothing produces "NaN".

exercises.explain: In a "Map", every key is unique: "set()" on an existing key replaces its value, and "get()" on a missing key yields "undefined".
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: There are three "set()" calls but only two distinct keys: the second "set("mug")" overwrites the first.
A key only keeps its latest value; 3 was replaced by 5.
A missing key returns "undefined" from "get()", not "null".

exercises.explain: "some()" answers "at least one?" and "every()" answers "all of them?"; both return a boolean, unlike "find()" and "filter()".
exercises.prompt: Which method replaces "___" so that this code prints true?
whyWrong: "every()" requires all scores to pass the test; 45 fails, so it returns false.
"find()" returns the first matching element, here 72, not a boolean.
"filter()" returns an array of the kept elements, [72, 90], not a boolean.

exercises.explain: Without a comparator, "sort()" sorts as strings ("1200" comes before "80"); for numbers, always pass "(a, b) => a - b".
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: That is the numeric order you would expect, but without a comparator "sort()" compares the values as strings, character by character.
Nothing asks for descending order; the default sort is ascending, but alphabetical.
"sort()" sorts in place: the array does not keep its original order.

exercises.explain: In a method chain, each step receives the result of the previous one: filter first, then sort what remains, then transform.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: The comparator "b.total - a.total" sorts from the largest to the smallest total: 300 before 120.
Order 2 (45) is removed by "filter()" before sorting, it cannot come back.
That would be the original order with no processing; the filter and the sort change everything.

exercises.explain: A closure keeps the variables of the function that created it; each call to the factory produces a closure with its own state.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: That would be the case if both counters shared one variable; each call to "makeCounter()" creates its own "count".
"clicksB" was never called before this line: its counter starts at 0 and goes to 1.
"++count" increments before returning: the third call returns 3, and the first call of "clicksB" returns 1, not 0.

exercises.explain: "sort()", "reverse()", "push()" or "splice()" mutate the array; to stay pure, copy first ("[...arr].sort()") or use "toSorted()".
exercises.prompt: In JavaScript, "sort()" mutates the array it is called on, whereas "map()" and "filter()" return a new array without touching the original.

exercises.explain: A "Set" drops duplicates; its size is read with "size", not "length", and "new Map()" expects key-value pairs.
exercises.prompt: Build a line that prints 2, the number of distinct leads.

exercises.explain: "fn(...args)" calls the function right away and hands its result to "setTimeout"; you must pass a function to run later: "() => fn(...args)".
exercises.prompt: This debounce never waits: "fn" runs immediately on every call instead of waiting for the delay to end. Which line is responsible?

exercises.explain: An error inside "try" jumps straight to "catch", and "finally" runs in every case: it is the place to clean up (hide a spinner, re-enable a button).
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: "JSON.parse" fails on "{lead}" (it is not valid JSON), so "ok" is never reached.
The "finally" block always runs, whether there was an error or not.
As soon as the error occurs, the rest of the "try" block is skipped: "ok" is not printed.

exercises.explain: "URLSearchParams" reads URL parameters without splitting the string by hand; "get()" returns the value or "null" when the key is missing.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: "get()" on a missing parameter returns "null", not "undefined" like a missing object property.
The leading "?" is ignored by "URLSearchParams", and "get()" returns only the value, not the key=value pair.
An empty string would only be returned for a present "utm_campaign=" with no value; here the parameter does not exist at all.

exercises.explain: "localStorage" and "sessionStorage" store strings only; for a boolean, a number or an object, use "JSON.stringify" when writing and "JSON.parse" when reading.
exercises.prompt: "sessionStorage" is empty at the start. What does this code print?
whyWrong: Web storage only keeps strings: the boolean is converted to ""true"" when saved.
The value read back is indeed a string, but ""true" === true" is false because the types differ.
"typeof" does not give "boolean": "getItem()" always returns a string (or "null").

exercises.explain: "document.cookie" behaves like an accumulator: writing to it adds or updates one cookie at a time, reading returns every accessible cookie as one "a=1; b=2" string.
exercises.prompt: At the start, the page has a single cookie and "document.cookie" is "consent=granted". What does this code print?
whyWrong: Assigning to "document.cookie" does not overwrite the list: it adds (or updates) a single cookie, so "consent" remains.
After the assignment, reading returns both cookies separated by "; ", so the length is 2.
The "consent=granted" cookie is still present in the string read back, so "includes" returns "true".

exercises.explain: Execution order: all synchronous code, then promise callbacks (microtasks), then timers, even at 0 ms.
exercises.prompt: In which order are the three words printed?
whyWrong: The code does not run line by line in writing order: the timer and the promise are deferred, the synchronous code goes first.
Even with a 0 ms delay, "setTimeout" runs after promise callbacks, which take priority.
A ".then" never runs before the current synchronous code finishes, even on an already resolved promise.

exercises.explain: "HttpOnly" can only be set server side and hides the cookie from JavaScript: it is sent with requests but a script cannot read it, which protects session tokens.
exercises.prompt: A session cookie set by the server with the "HttpOnly" attribute does not appear in "document.cookie", even when the script runs on the same domain.

exercises.explain: "fetch" does not reject on a 4xx or 5xx: the promise resolves, and "response.ok" (true for 200 to 299) tells you whether the request succeeded.
exercises.prompt: The API returns a 201 status when the lead is created and 422 when the email is invalid. What goes in place of "___" so that an error is thrown only when the status is not a success?
whyWrong: "status" is 201 or 422, two non-zero numbers that are always truthy: "!response.status" would never throw.
"response.success" does not exist: it is "undefined", so the error would be thrown even for the 201.
"response.error" does not exist either; besides, the logic would be reversed, we want to throw when the response is NOT good.

exercises.explain: A "throw" inside an "async" function becomes a rejected promise, caught by ".catch" or by a "try / catch" around an "await".
exercises.prompt: The API answers with an HTTP 404 status (the request completes, no network failure). What does this code print?
whyWrong: "sent" would require "response.ok" to be true; for a 404 it is false, and the "throw" stops the function.
"fetch" only rejects on a network failure or an unreachable URL; a 404 is a valid response, the error comes from our own "throw".
An error thrown inside an "async" function rejects the promise: the ".catch" runs, not the ".then", and it prints "err.message".

exercises.explain: "getItem" on a missing key returns "null", and "JSON.parse(null)" returns "null" without error; reading a property on "null" is what throws a "TypeError". Always check the value read back before using it.
exercises.prompt: "localStorage" is empty: the "utm" key was never saved. One line throws an error. Which one?

exercises.explain: "setTimeout(fn, ms)" runs "fn" once after "ms" milliseconds (1000 for one second); "setInterval" would repeat it forever.
exercises.prompt: Build a line that prints "go" once, one second after it runs.

exercises.explain: "process.env" only holds strings (or "undefined"); "??" supplies a fallback when the variable is missing, and you must convert with "Number()" yourself if you need a number.
exercises.prompt: This Node script runs with no "MAX_LEADS" environment variable set. What does it print?

code.src:
const limit = process.env.MAX_LEADS ?? "50";
console.log(typeof limit, limit);

whyWrong: The fallback is written in quotes, so it is a string; and even when set in the shell, an environment variable always arrives as a string.
"typeof" describes the type of "limit" after the "??", not the missing variable.
"??" is exactly what swaps "undefined" for the fallback, so "limit" is "50".

exercises.explain: "^1.4.0" means ">=1.4.0 <2.0.0": minor and patch versions may rise, the major is frozen.
exercises.prompt: Among these published versions of "chart-kit", which one can "npm install" pick?
whyWrong: The "^" stops right before the next major: 2.0.0 is excluded because a major bump may break the API.
1.3.7 is below the 1.4.0 minimum; a range never goes below the version written.
Sharing the minor 4 is not enough: the major is 2, outside the ">=1.4.0 <2.0.0" range.

exercises.explain: "process.argv" starts with the Node path then the script path; the real arguments begin at index 2, and "require("node:path")" loads a built-in module.
exercises.prompt: This script runs as "node import.js data/leads-q3.csv". What does it print?
whyWrong: "basename()" keeps only the last segment of the path; the "data/" folder is dropped.
The second argument of "basename()" strips the given extension.
"process.argv[1]" is the script; the first two slots are skipped, "file" is the third element.

exercises.explain: "~1.4.0" freezes the minor (">=1.4.0 <1.5.0") whereas "^1.4.0" only freezes the major ("<2.0.0").
exercises.prompt: Which range replaces "___" so that 1.4.7 is accepted but 1.5.0 is refused?
whyWrong: "^" lets the minor rise: 1.5.0 and even 1.9.0 would be accepted.
With no prefix, only the exact version 1.4.0 is accepted; 1.4.7 would be refused.
">=" has no upper bound: 1.5.0, 2.0.0 or 9.0.0 would all pass.

exercises.explain: npm recognizes the "pre" and "post" prefixes: "npm run build" chains "prebuild", "build" then "postbuild" when they exist, with no extra setup.
exercises.prompt: In "package.json", a script named "prebuild" is run automatically by npm right before "npm run build".

exercises.explain: TypeScript types vanish at compile time: an optional property that was never set simply does not exist in the resulting JavaScript object.
exercises.prompt: This TypeScript file is compiled and then run. What does it print?
whyWrong: Declaring "promo?" in the interface creates no property on the object: at runtime, "promo" does not exist in "p".
"p.promo" is indeed "undefined", but "??" replaces it with 0 before printing.
Neither part holds: "??" supplies 0, and the object never received a "promo" key.

exercises.explain: Once typed as "Lead", every property keeps its type: assigning a "number" to "email" (declared "string") is rejected at compile time, even though JavaScript would allow it.
exercises.prompt: TypeScript rejects exactly one of these lines. Which one?
lines: interface Lead { email: string; score: number }

exercises.explain: "a && b" returns "a" when it is falsy; since React renders numbers, a stray 0 leaks into the output. Use "items.length > 0 && …" or a ternary.
exercises.prompt: This component receives "items = []". What does the user see inside the paragraph?
whyWrong: React renders nothing for "false", "null" or "undefined", but 0 is a number and numbers are rendered.
"&&" stops at the first falsy operand: the "span" is never evaluated.
"&&" returns the operand itself, here the number 0, not a converted boolean.

exercises.explain: "count" is a constant of the current render: two "setCount(count + 1)" calls yield the same value. To accumulate, pass a function: "setCount(c => c + 1)".
exercises.prompt: The user clicks the button once. What does it show afterwards?
whyWrong: Both calls read the same "count" (0) captured at render time: each asks for "1", not "0 + 1" then "1 + 1".
"setCount" does schedule a re-render with the requested value, so the display changes.
"useState(0)" initializes "count" to 0, never to "undefined".

exercises.explain: In a React list, "key" must identify each item stably across renders: an id from the data, never a random value, and the displayed content must be a string or number, not an object.
exercises.prompt: Build the JSX list item that shows each product name with a stable, unique key.

exercises.explain: The dataLayer is a plain JavaScript array: "push" appends an object, and GTM reads the "event" key to know which trigger to fire and the other keys as parameters.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: "EUR" is the value of "currency"; the code reads "value", hence 120.
"last.event" returns the value stored under the "event" key, not the key’s name.
The object was just pushed, it is indeed the last item of the array and its "event" key exists.

exercises.explain: Open Graph tags ("og:title", "og:image", "og:description") drive the preview on Facebook, LinkedIn and most messaging apps; the "twitter:" tags only serve X, which falls back to "og:" when they are missing.
exercises.prompt: A visitor shares this page on Facebook. Which image shows up in the preview?
choices: og-guide.png and hero.jpg side by side
whyWrong: "twitter:image" is only read by X (Twitter); Facebook sticks to the "og:" tags.
Facebook only scans the page’s "" tags when there is no "og:image" tag at all.
A share preview shows a single image, the one declared in "og:image".

exercises.explain: For a "Product", Google reads the price inside "offers": an "Offer" with "price" (number, decimal point) and "priceCurrency" (ISO code); the rating comes from "aggregateRating" and is never mistaken for the price.
exercises.prompt: What price will Google read from this JSON-LD?
choices: None: the price must be a direct property of "Product"
None: "priceValidUntil" is missing, the offer is rejected
whyWrong: "priceCurrency" expects a three-letter ISO 4217 code such as "EUR", not a symbol.
In schema.org the price lives in the "Offer" attached to the product through "offers"; "Product" has no "price" property.
"priceValidUntil" is only recommended: leaving it out yields a warning, not an error.

exercises.explain: "gtag()" pushes its arguments as they are into the dataLayer. "consent default" sets the starting state before any tag, "consent update" only carries the permissions that change; the others keep their previous value.
exercises.prompt: What does this code print?
whyWrong: The Google tag does keep "ad_storage" denied internally, but the object pushed by "update" only holds the keys it was given.
That is the first call; the code reads the last item of the array, that is the "update".
"consent" sits at index 0; "c[1]" is the second argument, "update".

exercises.explain: A pixel fires as soon as it is loaded and "track" is called, unless you stop it: at Meta, "fbq('consent', 'revoke')" before "init" holds events back until the "grant" triggered by the CMP.
exercises.prompt: The Meta pixel is loaded right before these lines. Does the "PageView" reach Meta as soon as the page loads, before any click?
choices: No: nothing is sent before "grant", so not before the click on "accept"
Yes: "init" then "track" send the PageView right away
No: "revoke" disables the pixel for good, even after the click
whyWrong: That would be true without the first line; "revoke" called before "init" blocks sending.
The Meta pixel has no "cookieless" mode: with consent revoked, it sends nothing.
"grant" re-enables the pixel; "revoke" is a pause, not an uninstall.

exercises.explain: GTM does not read a push in isolation: it merges every push into a persistent data model, deeply for objects. That is why Google recommends "dataLayer.push({ ecommerce: null })" before each e-commerce event, so an old cart does not leak into the next one.
exercises.prompt: A GA4 tag fires on the "purchase" event and reads the data layer variable "ecommerce.currency" (version 2). What value does GA4 receive?
choices: Nothing: the tag does not fire, "currency" is missing from the second push
whyWrong: It would be "undefined" if GTM only read the last object; it actually merges every push into its data model, nested objects included.
89.9 is the new value of "ecommerce.value", not of "ecommerce.currency".
The trigger only looks at the "event" key; missing parameters do not block the tag.

exercises.explain: A "FAQPage" valid for Google holds "Question" items with "name" and "acceptedAnswer", and each "Answer" must carry "text"; an unknown property is ignored, a missing required one makes the block ineligible.
exercises.prompt: What replaces "___" so that Google accepts this FAQPage?

code.src:
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "FAQPage",
  "mainEntity": [{
    "@type": "Question",
    "name": "What is the delivery time?",
    "acceptedAnswer": { "@type": "Answer", "___": "48 hours in mainland France." }
  }]
}
</script>

whyWrong: "answer" is not a schema.org property; the answer is already the "Answer" object, its content is called "text".
"description" exists on every "Thing", but Google requires "text" on an "Answer" to display it.
"content" is not an "Answer" property; it would simply be ignored and "text" would still be missing.

exercises.explain: The hero image is usually the LCP element itself: delaying it delays LCP. You do the opposite, "fetchpriority='high'" on that "" or a "", and keep "loading='lazy'" for images below the fold.
exercises.prompt: Adding "loading='lazy'" to the hero image at the top of the home page improves LCP, since the browser has less to download at first.

exercises.explain: A JSON-LD is JSON first: a date is a quoted string ("2026-03-01"). Without quotes, 2026-03-01 is neither a number nor a string and the whole block is ignored.
exercises.prompt: Google rejects this JSON-LD: a single line makes it invalid. Which one?

exercises.explain: A GTM push takes an object in curly braces: the "event" key names the event, the other keys carry the parameters. Square brackets would create an array, which GTM could not read as an event.
exercises.prompt: Build a push that sends GTM the "purchase" event with a value of 89.9.
